opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key word in your question is "compose." When a diffusion model generates a face it has never seen, it isn't interpolating between training images in pixel space. That would give you blurry averages, ghostly superpositions. What it produces is sharp and coherent, so it must have learned something about how images are *built*.

My view, which comes from the work we've been doing with simple models of data, is that natural data is hierarchical and compositional. A face is made of parts: eyes, a nose, a mouth. Those are made of sub-parts, edges, textures, down to pixels. And at each level there's a lot of freedom. There are many "synonyms," many different low-level configurations that play the same role at the next level up. Two noses can look quite different in pixels and still be equally valid noses in a face.

If a model captures that structure, the rules for how parts combine at each scale, then it can generate new faces simply by making new combinations that respect the rules. It doesn't need to have seen that particular combination. That's where creativity comes from, if you want to call it that: the space of valid combinations is combinatorially huge compared to the training set.

The question then is how a network learns these rules from a finite number of examples, and this is where it gets interesting. We studied this with what we call the Random Hierarchy Model, a synthetic generative grammar where we control the hierarchy precisely. What you find is that the network learns the structure level by level. Local correlations between neighbouring features are detectable from relatively few samples, so the low-level rules are learned first. Once you've grouped synonyms together, the problem at the next level becomes smaller, and you can learn the next level with a manageable number of examples. The sample complexity grows polynomially rather than exponentially with the dimension, which is really the only way to escape the curse of dimensionality.

Diffusion gives you a beautiful window into this. If you take a real image, add noise up to some time *t*, and then let the model denoise, you're probing different levels of the hierarchy. At small noise, only low-level details change: textures, fine edges. At large noise, you change the high-level class, so you might get a completely different image. And in between, there's something quite sharp, almost a phase transition, where the high-level identity is preserved but the parts are reassembled. You keep "a face," maybe even the pose, but the eyes or the mouth are swapped for different, still consistent versions. In our hierarchical models we can compute this transition and show that the changes come in correlated chunks whose size grows as you approach it, a bit like critical phenomena in physics. And we see the same signatures in real diffusion models trained on images, and actually in text too.

So, to sum up: a diffusion model composes new faces because it has learned a hierarchical grammar of faces. It learned it from the bottom up, exploiting local correlations, and at generation time it builds images from the top down, choosing high-level structure first and filling in compatible details. Novelty is just a new sentence in that grammar.

r001.rationale: It says the model learns rules for combining facial parts and can generate new faces through new valid combinations, including reassembled eyes and mouths.

r002.rationale: It describes testable behavior across noise levels, including a sharp transition and correlated changes in chunks, and says these signatures are observed in real diffusion models.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that it's genuinely puzzling. A diffusion model is trained on, say, a few hundred thousand faces, and yet it produces faces that are clearly not in the training set, that combine features in ways it has never seen. So the naive picture, that the model just memorizes and interpolates between examples, cannot be the whole story. If you were simply interpolating in pixel space you would get blurry averages, not sharp new faces.

The way I like to think about it comes from physics, and in particular from the idea of hierarchy and compositionality. Natural data, images, language, has this structure where high-level features are built from lower-level features, which are built from even lower-level ones. A face is made of eyes, a nose, a mouth, arranged in a certain way. Each eye is made of an iris, an eyelid, lashes. And the crucial point is that the low-level components are, to a good approximation, interchangeable. You can take the shape of one person's eyes and the mouth of another, and the result is still a face.

So we built toy models of this, generative models of data with an explicit hierarchical and compositional structure, something like a probabilistic context-free grammar. You have a root symbol, it produces children according to some rules, those children produce their own children, and so on down to the leaves, which are the pixels. In this setting we can actually compute what a diffusion model should do, and compare with what trained networks actually do.

And what emerges is quite nice. The diffusion process has a time, the noise level, and as you add noise you destroy information at different scales. Small amounts of noise wipe out the fine, low-level details but leave the high-level structure intact. Large amounts of noise destroy the high-level structure too. Now, when you denoise, the network at each stage has to reconstruct the information that was lost. And what we find is that there is a phase transition. Below a certain noise level, the model reconstructs essentially the same image, just cleaning up the details. Above that noise level, the identity of the top-level features changes, you get a different class, a different face, but the low-level grammar, the way the parts are assembled, is preserved.

So composition is really happening at the level of these intermediate latent variables. The model learns the rules at each level of the hierarchy, which parts go with which, and the forward-backward diffusion process lets you resample the high-level choices while respecting the low-level consistency. That's what gives you a new face that looks coherent rather than a collage.

The other piece, which I think is important, is the sample complexity. If you had to learn the full joint distribution of pixels directly, you would need an astronomical number of examples, exponential in the dimension. But if the data has this hierarchical structure, you only need to learn the correlations between a parent and its children at each level, and that scales polynomially. We can actually predict the number of training examples needed, as a function of the depth and the branching factor of the grammar, and we see that U-Net-type architectures indeed learn in that regime. Below that scale they memorize, above it they generalize and compose.

So, to answer directly: I understand it as the model learning a hierarchy of local composition rules, with the noise level acting as a knob that selects which levels get resampled. The faces are new because the high-level combinations are new, but they are convincing because the lower-level rules, which are shared across all faces, are respected. And the beautiful thing is that this is not a hand-wavy metaphor, it is something you can write down and test in simple synthetic models, and it seems to carry over to real images and even to text.

r001.rationale: It says new faces arise from new combinations of high-level choices while shared low-level facial parts and assembly rules are preserved.

r002.rationale: It describes the account as something that can be written down and tested in synthetic models, and gives testable predictions about sample complexity and when models memorize versus generalize and compose.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is what we mean by a new face. A model can generate an image that is different from every image in its training set, but that alone doesn’t tell us how much it has learned about the structure of faces.

One way to think about composition is that the model learns features and relationships between features that can be reused. It doesn’t need to have seen every possible combination of eyes, nose, and mouth. But these elements cannot be assembled independently either: their shapes, their positions, the lighting, all have to be consistent.

In a diffusion model, you start from noise and progressively remove it. The learned denoising process guides the image toward configurations that look like the training data. If it has learned relationships that apply across many examples, that process can produce a coherent face whose particular combination of features was never observed.

So the question, for me, is when the model learns these reusable relationships, rather than simply retaining individual examples. What properties of the data, and how much data, allow that transition? That is where composition becomes an interesting scientific problem.

r001.rationale: It says the model learns reusable facial features and relationships, then can produce a coherent face with a feature combination never observed.

r002.rationale: It frames composition as a scientific problem and poses questions about data and learning, but does not state that the account yields nontrivial, empirically testable predictions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the model does not learn a face as one indivisible object. It learns statistical relationships at many different scales: the local structure of an eye, how eyes are positioned relative to a nose, and the overall geometry of a face. During generation, these constraints have to become mutually consistent.

So composing a new face doesn't necessarily mean copying pieces of different training images and sticking them together. You start with noise, and the denoising process progressively organizes it into something compatible with the relationships the model has learned. There can be many configurations that satisfy those relationships without corresponding to a particular face in the training set.

The interesting question is when that happens—when the model learns enough shared structure to generate new combinations, rather than simply reproducing examples. And a realistic-looking face alone doesn't establish which of those mechanisms is operating.

r001.rationale: It describes learned local facial structure and spatial relationships becoming mutually consistent in new combinations during generation.

r002.rationale: It raises a question about when new combinations occur, but does not say this account yields nontrivial, empirically testable predictions.
